abraham-lincoln-collection.title: Kiriakou's Abraham Lincoln collection
abraham-lincoln-collection.summary: John Kiriakou's private collection of Abraham Lincoln relics, assembled at auction over many years and governed by a strict standard of provenance: a blood-soaked fragment of the pillowcase Lincoln died on, wallpaper from the Petersen House death room, a swatch of Mary Todd Lincoln's funeral dress, and wood from the gallows on which the conspirators were hanged.
dyk: ...that [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) owns a blood-soaked fragment of the pillowcase Abraham Lincoln died on, and can trace its chain of custody from the doctor who removed the bullet from Lincoln's brain through a governor of [Indiana](/wiki/india) to the auction where he bought it?

...that the only Lincoln lot [Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) says he truly regrets losing was the original key to Lincoln's tomb, which went for close to $10,000 at a 2009 Dallas auction — his wife's objection being that it was, in the end, [just a key](/wiki/lincolns-last-turd)?
abraham-lincoln-collection.body:
[John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) is a private collector of Abraham Lincoln material, a pursuit he describes as dating to childhood and grounded in the view that Lincoln was *"the greatest president in American history"* and *"the kind of person that we should want to be like."* He buys at major auction houses and treats documented provenance as the governing rule of the field.<Cite t="1:20:45" /><Cite t="1:28:04" />

## The collection

Kiriakou's holdings, as he describes them, include an 11½-inch strip of wallpaper from the room at the Petersen guest house where Lincoln died; a swatch of the black dress Mary Todd Lincoln wore to her husband's funeral; a piece of the wood from the gallows on which the Lincoln conspirators were hanged; a ballot from Ohio in the 1860 election bearing Lincoln's name; and a framed fragment of the blood-soaked pillowcase on which Lincoln died. He keeps the pieces framed and hung rather than in a dedicated room.<Cite t="1:20:45" /><Cite t="1:21:17" /><Cite t="1:29:06" />

## Provenance

Provenance — the documented chain by which an object passed from Lincoln himself to its present owner — is the discipline Kiriakou treats as definitional: *"you have to be able to document from Lincoln himself how it got to you."* He offers the pillowcase fragment as the model. Mr Petersen, who owned the house in which Lincoln died, cut the pillowcase into pieces with scissors and gave one to the doctor who had removed the bullet from Lincoln's brain; the doctor gave it to his daughter, who married a governor of Indiana; it descended through that family until they sold it at auction, where Kiriakou bought it.<Cite t="1:20:45" /><Cite t="1:21:47" /><Cite t="1:22:19" />

The same standard is what makes [Lincoln's last turd](/wiki/lincolns-last-turd) the collection's defining negative case. Kiriakou's wife objected to that lot precisely on provenance grounds — a sideshow museum's display card documents nothing — and the DNA analysis that followed the sale vindicated her.

## The tomb key

The loss Kiriakou says he still regrets is the original key to Lincoln's tomb, offered at a large Lincoln sale at Heritage Auctions in Dallas in 2009. He bid to somewhere between $3,600 and $3,800; the key sold for close to $10,000. His wife's assessment was that it was a key.<Cite t="1:28:04" /><Cite t="1:28:35" />

## Authentication and the wider market

Kiriakou extends the provenance principle beyond his own collecting to the art market generally, and is a sceptic of the attribution of *Salvator Mundi* to Leonardo da Vinci — the painting bought at auction for roughly $450 million by a buyer later understood to be Mohammed bin Salman. His objection is the one he applies to his own lots: the chain of custody was never established. *"I think Mohammed bin Salman got ripped off."* He allows that the expert who authenticated it may have been acting in good faith under confirmation bias, finding a Leonardo being the thing everyone in that line of work fantasises about.<Cite t="1:29:39" /><Cite t="1:33:17" /><Cite t="1:34:20" /><Cite t="1:34:50" />

He notes that an old master painting of the sixteenth or seventeenth century can still be had for around $1,500 if the attribution is uncertain and it is catalogued as "school of" or "circle of" — the crack through which the *Salvator Mundi* dealers slipped.<Cite t="1:31:11" />
